sections.html:
Haverhill is a city in Essex County on the Merrimack River, right at the New Hampshire border. It is about 35 miles north of Boston and 17 miles from the Atlantic Ocean, and the 2020 census counted 67,787 residents.

The city covers 35.7 square miles, of which 33 are land, and it is the largest city or town in Essex County. It borders Merrimac, West Newbury, Groveland, Boxford, North Andover and Methuen, plus Salem, Atkinson and Plaistow in New Hampshire. The Merrimack separates the Bradford section from the rest of the city.

Haverhill was settled in 1640 as Pentucket, an Algonquian word for place of the winding river, and incorporated in 1641. It became a city in 1870.

Shoe manufacturing built the city. By the end of 1913, one tenth of the shoes made in the United States came from Haverhill, which earned it the nickname Queen Slipper City. A great fire on February 17, 1882, destroyed much of the mill district, with about 300 businesses lost.

Bradford was a separate town until January 1, 1897, when it joined Haverhill. Bradford remains the only Massachusetts town, apart from those joined to Boston, that was annexed by a neighboring city. In the 1950s and 1960s, urban renewal demolished much of downtown, but the Highlands district still has Victorian mansions from the shoe boom.

sections.h2: Which parts of Haverhill matter to a seller?
sections.html:
Haverhill is made of several districts with their own character, and a buyer will ask which one your house is in. The city has a downtown along the river, the Highlands next to it, Bradford across the Merrimack, Ward Hill and the historic district of Rocks Village.

  • Downtown: rezoned to encourage artist live-work lofts and educational uses, with a parking garage, boardwalk and boat docks added along the river.
  • The Highlands: a district beside downtown with Victorian mansions built in the shoe boom.
  • Bradford: the area on the far side of the Merrimack, home to the Bradford MBTA station.
  • Rocks Village: a historic district listed among the city's early architecture, alongside the 1691 Kimball Tavern.

Winnekenni Park, a conservation area with Winnekenni Castle and Lake Saltonstall, is one of the city's best known open spaces.

sections.h2: What does Haverhill's housing look like?
sections.html:
Haverhill's housing ranges from colonial-era houses to Victorian mansions and converted mill lofts. The 2020 census counted 26,696 households and 27,927 housing units, and 4.4 percent of units were vacant.

A homeowner vacancy rate of 0.8 percent indicates that very few owned homes sat empty at the time of the census. Downtown rezoning has also converted old factories into loft apartments and condominiums, with about $150 million in public and private investment in the old factory district.

sections.h2: Who runs Haverhill, and who lives there?
sections.html:
Haverhill has a strong mayor and a nine-member city council. Melinda Barrett became mayor in 2024 and is the first woman to hold the office.

The 2020 census recorded a median age of 39.7, with 21 percent of residents under 18 and 15.6 percent age 65 or older. About 23.6 percent identified as Hispanic or Latino. The population grew 11.3 percent between 2010 and 2020, and the Census Bureau's 2024 estimate is 68,291. Steady growth usually means buyers keep looking, though it does not guarantee any price.

sections.h2: How is the Haverhill terrain and climate relevant to a house?
sections.html:
Glaciers shaped Haverhill, leaving drumlins, eskers, kettle ponds and gravel deposits across the city. The highest point is Ayers Hill, a drumlin of at least 335 feet. The city is drained by the Little and Merrimack rivers.

Haverhill's normals show about 49.6 inches of precipitation and 57.8 inches of snow a year. The record high is 105 degrees Fahrenheit and the record low is minus 21. Heavy snow on roofs, ice in gutters and basement dampness near the river are the normal concerns for homes here.

sections.h2: How do you get around Haverhill?
sections.html:
Interstate 495 runs through Haverhill with five exits, and Routes 97, 108, 110, 113 and 125 cross the city. Routes 108 and 125 end at the New Hampshire line and continue into that state.

  • MBTA Commuter Rail serves the Haverhill and Bradford stations on the Haverhill/Reading Line to North Station.
  • Amtrak also serves the Haverhill station, with service to Portland, Maine and Boston.
  • MeVa Transit provides local bus service in and beyond Haverhill.
  • Logan International Airport in Boston is the nearest international airport.

When you describe a house to a buyer, give the distance to the nearest I-495 exit or rail station.

sections.h2: Which schools and colleges are in Haverhill?
sections.html:
Haverhill Public Schools runs the city's public schools. Whittier Regional Vocational Technical High School takes students by lottery from Haverhill and nearby towns, and Hill View Montessori Charter Public School serves kindergarten through eighth grade. Northern Essex Community College has its main campus here, and Northpoint Bible College is also in the city.

The city has rebuilt Hunking Middle School in Bradford and is working on a new campus for the Dr. A.B. Consentino Middle School.

sections.h2: When are Haverhill property taxes due?
sections.html:
Haverhill's official page says real estate and personal property tax payments are due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. Interest accrues at 14 percent on bills not paid on the due dates.

Preliminary bills are estimates based on the previous fiscal year's actual net bill. The city's formula is last year's actual tax times 2.5 percent, added to the actual, divided by four. Unpaid balances after May 1 can lead to a tax lien, and new liens after November 2024 carry 8 percent interest. Liens are recorded with the Registry of Deeds.

When a property changes hands after the January 1 assessment, the bill stays in the January 1 owner's name. The new owner must contact the Assessors at 978-374-2316 for a duplicate bill. Abatement applications must reach the Assessors on or before February 1. See the tax payment page.

sections.h2: What does a Haverhill smoke and carbon monoxide inspection cost?
sections.html:
The Haverhill Fire Prevention Office inspects smoke and carbon monoxide detectors before each residential sale closes, under M.G.L. Chapter 148, Section 26F and 26F 1/2. Inspections are done on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and only a limited number can be done each day.

  • One residential unit: $50
  • Two units: $100
  • Three to six units: $150
  • Seven or more units: $500

The certificate is valid for 60 days, and the city will not schedule the inspection until payment is received. You will get an email with the date and a call with the appointment time. Applications and details are on the fire department's page, or call 978-373-8460.

sections.h2: What do Haverhill sellers commonly face?
sections.html:
Many Haverhill sellers own older houses that need updating or inherited property they cannot easily manage. Because the certificate is valid for only 60 days, you want to book the inspection close enough to closing that it will not lapse.

A cash sale as-is can fit when the house needs work or the owner cannot manage repairs. For other owners, a listing may bring more money if the home is in good condition. Weigh both before you decide.

faqs.a: Yes. Haverhill is the largest city or town in Essex County, located on the Merrimack River at the New Hampshire border.

faqs.q: When are Haverhill property tax payments due?
faqs.a: The city lists February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1 as the due dates, with 14 percent interest on late payments.

faqs.q: How long is a Haverhill smoke detector certificate valid?
faqs.a: It is valid for 60 days. Haverhill inspects on Tuesdays and Thursdays and does not schedule until payment is received.

faqs.q: How much is the smoke and carbon monoxide inspection for a single-family home in Haverhill?
faqs.a: The fee for one residential unit is $50, according to the Fire Department's page.

faqs.q: Who gets the tax bill after I sell my Haverhill house?
faqs.a: The bill stays in the name of the owner as of January 1. The new owner contacts the Assessors for a duplicate, and closing adjustments handle the split.
